newsitem.title: USA: TVA seeks antitrust probe of rival U.S. utilities.
newsitem.headline: TVA seeks antitrust probe of rival U.S. utilities.

text.p: Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) said Wednesday it has asked the U.S. Justice Department to look into whether rival, publicly-traded power companies are breaking antitrust laws by seeking to rein in TVA's sales.

"It appears from these private utilities' own documents that their activities are to undermine TVA's ability to compete," TVA General Counsel Edward Christenbury said in a letter to Attorney General Janet Reno.
"(There) may be a question of whether the activities of these utilities are designed to prevent TVA from carrying out its mission under the TVA Act."

TVA, created by a federal mandate in the 1930s, seeks to provide power at the lowest possible cost. It is the biggest supplier of electricity in the U.S., with a total generation capacity of 28,123 megawatts and 1996 sales of $5.7 billion.
"TVA's power program is completely self-supporting, with no federal support of any kind," said spokesman Frank Cason at TVA's Knoxville, Tenn., headquarters.
The letter to Janet Reno comes just six days after Southern Company, Duke Power Co, and a unit of Entergy Corp filed a lawsuit against TVA in a U.S. District Court in Birmingham, Alabama.
The lawsuit alleges TVA has overstepped its federal mandate by using its Tennessee Valley customers as outlets for selling power to customers beyond its designated territory.

The three utilities argue TVA, as a protected agency, enjoys competitive advantages denied to private utilities seeking to expand their own revenue base as the U.S. moves to deregulate its $200 billion a year electricity industry.

Christenbury, in a statement issued by TVA, said Southern, Duke, Entergy, American Electric Power Co (AEP), and Carolina Power & Light Co had formed an association called TVA Watch or the TVA Reform Alliance.

"We are just trying to be sure that when competition begins, it is on a balanced playing field, and that we are not competing against a quasi-government agency that is subsidized and in the marketplace," said Pat Hemlepp, spokesman for AEP in Columbus, Ohio.
"Having one group out there that doesn't exist in the same competitive environment doesn't help, and that is why we are part of the TVA Reform Alliance," he said.

TVA Chairman Craven Crowell, in a meeting Tuesday with members of Congress representing the Tennessee Valley, said "TVA is under more intense attack from private utilities than at any time in its history.
"Private utilities don't want to be benchmarked against TVA's low-cost power and efficient operations; rather they apparently want to take our customers," Crowell said.

Asked what the next step will be in what promises to be a lengthy legal battle, TVA's Cason said: "We'll have to see what the Justice Department investigation shows. We expect them to look at it, but there's no guarantees on what they'll do with it."
